outline.description: Sets out the alleged pump‑and‑dump scheme, the charges brought, the district court’s dismissal, and the Fifth Circuit’s de novo review on appeal.
subtopics: Alleged conduct: coordinated purchase, promotional ‘pump’ via false social‑media posts, and secret ‘dump’ for profit
Defendants and platforms; public persona as skilled traders; alleged $114 million in profits
Charges: 18 U.S.C. § 1349 (conspiracy) and 18 U.S.C. §§ 1348 & 2 (securities fraud and aiding/abetting)
District court ruling: indictment fails to allege deprivation of traditional property; focuses only on loss of valuable economic information
Government’s timely appeal
Standard of review: de novo; taking indictment’s allegations as true; requirements for indictment sufficiency (enumerate elements, fair notice, double‑jeopardy protection)

outline.chapter_title: Governing Law: Securities Fraud under § 1348 and Indictment Sufficiency
outline.description: Explains the elements of securities fraud as interpreted through mail/wire fraud jurisprudence and the standards for a valid indictment.
subtopics: Text of § 1348: schemes to defraud and schemes to obtain money or property in connection with securities
Borrowing from mail and wire fraud: Greenlaw and Evans as interpretive anchors
Elements: (1) scheme to defraud with material misrepresentation to obtain value; (2) intent to deceive and to cause harm resulting from deceit
Supreme Court synthesis: Kousisis and Ciminelli—deception plus obtaining money or property as an object
Indictment sufficiency: alleging each material element; fair notice; double‑jeopardy bar (Gaytan; Guzman‑Ocampo; Fontenot; Crow)

outline.chapter_title: Issue 1: Does the Indictment Allege a Scheme to Defraud (Traditional Property) or Only Loss of Information?
outline.description: Analyzes whether the indictment impermissibly relies on a right‑to‑control theory barred by Ciminelli, or properly alleges fraudulent inducement to part with money.
subtopics: Ciminelli’s holding: the ‘right‑to‑control’ theory (loss of valuable economic information) is not a traditional property interest
Key distinction: right‑to‑control versus fraudulent‑inducement theories
Kousisis’s validation of fraudulent‑inducement: using material misstatements to induce transactions that transfer money or property
Application to the indictment: alleged misrepresentations about positions and price potential intended to induce followers to buy securities (spend money)
Conclusion on Element 1: indictment alleges deprivation of money/property through fraudulent inducement, not mere loss of information

outline.chapter_title: Issue 2: Intent to Defraud—Must the Government Allege Intended Economic Harm?
outline.description: Explores whether intent to profit without intending victim loss defeats the fraud charge, and applies Kousisis to reject a net‑loss requirement.
subtopics: Defendants’ argument: intent to enrich themselves, not to harm followers; followers received market‑value securities
Kousisis’s rule: fraud is complete when defendant seeks to obtain victim’s money or property, even absent intended or actual net economic loss
Supporting Fifth Circuit precedent: Baker rejects mirror‑image loss‑gain requirement
Application to the indictment: allegations of false posts designed to induce purchases show intent to obtain followers’ money; ‘had money in mind’
Rejection of harm requirement: receipt of market‑value securities does not negate fraudulent inducement
Persuasive authority: Seventh Circuit’s Smith applying Kousisis in similar context

outline.description: States the court’s holding and discusses what it means for future prosecutions involving market‑manipulation schemes and social‑media promotions.
subtopics: Holding: indictment sufficiently alleges both a scheme to defraud and intent to defraud; reversal of dismissal and remand
What survives to trial: government must still prove material misrepresentations, scheme, and intent beyond a reasonable doubt
Doctrinal takeaways: fraudulent inducement is a valid theory protecting money/property; no net‑loss requirement; right‑to‑control remains impermissible
Implications for social‑media promoters: misstatements that induce purchases can satisfy § 1348 where obtaining money is an object of the scheme
Limits: opinion does not relax materiality or scienter; focuses on sufficiency at the pleading stage under established standards
